part_title: PartyRock — Building a No-Code AI Playground
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 15 through 15 individually in source order, verifying visible labels, workflows, examples, access-control boundaries, and service distinctions; rewritten as balanced-length teaching narration.

scenes.title: PartyRock app playground
scenes.narration: The final slide compares two different ways to build generative AI applications without writing a traditional full application. Look at PartyRock on the left. A learner describes an idea such as summarizing product reviews and listing pros and cons. PartyRock offers visual no-code widgets for prompts, data input and output. The resulting experimental app uses foundation models powered by Amazon Bedrock, and the slide emphasizes quick browser-based exploration without needing an AWS account to get started. That makes PartyRock useful for learning and trying personal prototypes, not for handling confidential company documents. Now move to Amazon Q Apps on the right. An employee needs a reusable internal application based on organization knowledge such as HR policies or product FAQs. Q Apps provides a natural-language building experience, connections to approved company content and tools, controlled access, and a way to share workflows with colleagues. The lower examples reinforce the decision: use PartyRock for a study assistant built from your own non-sensitive notes, or Q Apps for an internal HR-policy assistant with company-managed access. These are not interchangeable choices. Ask whether the goal is rapid experimentation or a governed, repeatable enterprise workflow.
